clue.text: Great care home keeping father and son apart

indicators.note: a word that keeps two others is holding them, one at each side of itself
apart says the two outer pieces are separated by what sits between them

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
S is the standard abbreviation for son
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A care home is praised for keeping a squabbling father and son away from each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great care home' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'care'; to take pains is to take great care.
explanation.definitionFit: Pains, in the plural, means careful effort, as in the idiom taking pains over something.

clue.text: Nut's top religious books showing proof of Creator?

parts.note: nut is slang for the head, and the pate is the top of the head
NT is the New Testament, a set of religious books

explanation.surface: Holy scriptures at the top of a pile are offered as evidence for God the Creator.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C suggests God; here the creator is simply an inventor, and the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A patent is the official document recognising an inventor's rights, so it serves as proof of who created something.

clue.text: Attribute wrinkled up with time

indicators.note: something wrinkled has been creased out of its smooth shape, so these letters are rumpled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wrinkles are put down to the passing of the years.
explanation.definitionFit: To impute something is to attribute it to a cause or a person, both verbs of assigning responsibility.

clue.text: Potentially never-ending series then, each set of years

parts.note: so, as in 'and so', means then or therefore
a pop is a casual way of saying each, as in five pounds a pop
an era is a period of years

explanation.surface: Someone describes a series that seems to run forever, one era after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pop' for each is informal: tickets at ten pounds a pop.
explanation.definitionFit: Television soap operas such as long-running serial dramas can continue for decades with no planned ending.

clue.text: Current advice in recession, sell? Don't be dumb

indicators.note: something in recession is going back, so the preceding words are read from the end to the start

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current in physics
tips are pieces of advice
to tout is to try to sell, as touts do with tickets

explanation.surface: A financial adviser is pressed for the latest guidance on selling during an economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current advice in recession' sounds like economics; current is the physics symbol, and recession turns the first two pieces round.
explanation.definitionFit: Spit it out is an idiom urging a hesitant speaker to say what they mean rather than stay silent.

clue.text: Wave from spot in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is a place of listening, so the word is taken as it is heard rather than as it is spelt

parts.note: to spot something is to see it

explanation.surface: An audience member waves from their seat in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Spot pretends to be a noun, a place in the hall; it is the verb, to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea can mean a single large wave, as sailors say a heavy sea broke over the deck.

clue.text: Conservative cracking nuts was Etonian genius

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece goes inside the other
nuts means crazy, so the following words are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A Tory who has gone mad turns out to have been a brilliant old boy of Eton.
explanation.walkthrough: Newton actually went to the King's School, Grantham, not Eton, so the surface is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton, the physicist of gravity and calculus, is a byword for scientific brilliance.

clue.text: Press claim to be the greatest footballer, nearly?

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the phrase loses its final letter

parts.note: a claim to be something begins 'I'm', the contraction of I am
the Brazilian forward Pelé is widely called the greatest footballer of all time

explanation.surface: A footballer tells the newspapers that he is almost the best player ever.
explanation.walkthrough: Press looks like the newspapers; it is the verb, to urge.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel someone is to drive or urge them on, just as to press them is to push them to act.

clue.text: Dear fellow died in our lift, putting that out of order

indicators.note: something out of order is not in its proper sequence, so all these letters are rearranged

parts.note: d. is the abbreviation for died in dates and records
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dear old man has died in the block's elevator, so it is put out of service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' is what a sign on a broken lift says, which hides its role as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Old fruit is a dated, jovial British form of address for a friend, like old chap or old bean.

clue.text: Blooming years passed wearing shackles

indicators.note: something worn is enclosed by what is worn, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: ties are bonds or fetters
went means passed, as time went by

explanation.surface: Someone's youthful years slipped by while they were held back in chains.
explanation.definitionFit: One's twenties, the decade from twenty to twenty-nine, are thought of as the bloom or prime of life.

clue.text: Act given star billing, for best performance by a theatrical dog

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the headline comedian in a show

definitions.text: best performance by a theatrical dog
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the theatre's own version of top dog, the leading performer

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an animal act winning an award; the second half playfully renders 'top dog' in show-business slang, where a banana is a comic.
explanation.definitionFit: Top banana is American theatre slang for the star comedian of a show, and by extension the leading person anywhere.

clue.text: One that might leave fingerprint on priest

parts.note: the pad of a finger is the fleshy tip that leaves a print
re means on or concerning, as in business letters

explanation.surface: A detective finds a clergyman's fingerprint and wonders who left it.
explanation.definitionFit: Padre is the informal term for a chaplain, especially a military one, so a kind of priest.

clue.text: Wimbledon etc ordinarily entertaining tennis supporter

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to have them inside, so the run of letters is held within these words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Wimbledon, all of etc and the start of ordinarily

explanation.surface: Wimbledon and similar tournaments usually provide some fun for tennis fans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tennis supporter' looks like a fan in the crowd; it is the cable that holds up the net.
explanation.definitionFit: The net cord is the cable along the top of a tennis net, literally supporting it.

clue.text: Greek bigamist's requirement?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unintelligible talk, as in 'it's all Greek to me'
second meaning: two wives, since dutch is old London slang for a wife

explanation.walkthrough: Greek looks like a nationality; it means gibberish. Dutch for wife comes from Cockney rhyming slang, duchess of Fife.
explanation.definitionFit: Double Dutch is British slang for incomprehensible language, the same sense as saying something is all Greek.

clue.text: Criminal shifted strip club's entire contents

indicators.note: shifted means the letters are moved around into a new order
the entire contents of a phrase are everything between its first and last letters

parts.note: taken as written, the two words run together

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer is pictured whisking away everything inside a strip club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entire contents' drops the S and B that bound STRIPCLUB, leaving TRIPCLU, which 'shifted' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A culprit is the person guilty of an offence, a wrongdoer.

clue.text: Profitable forging Vermeer at uni

indicators.note: forging means faking or hammering into shape, so the letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student makes money by faking Dutch masterpieces at university.
explanation.definitionFit: Remunerative work pays well, so it is profitable for the one doing it.

clue.text: Skip wearing silver trousers all over the place

indicators.note: used as a verb, to trouser something is to pocket it, so one part holds the other inside

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
to bound is to leap or skip
wearing a coat is being in it

explanation.surface: Someone skips about in shiny silver trousers everywhere they go.
explanation.walkthrough: Trousers looks like clothing; it is the verb, to pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abounding exists in great quantity, so it is to be found everywhere.

clue.text: Ancient poet stuck with an unusually old keyboard

indicators.note: stuck with suggests something lodged firmly inside another, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Virgil was the Roman poet of the Aeneid

indicators.note: unusually means in an odd way, so this little word is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A classical poet is lumbered with a strange antique instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The virginal was a small harpsichord-like keyboard instrument popular in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

clue.text: Star put in jeopardy beneath a wobbly set

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady, so these letters shake into another order
in a down entry, a piece placed beneath another simply follows it

parts.note: taken as written
the word set, rearranged
to risk something is to put it in jeopardy

explanation.surface: An actor's career is endangered by a shaky film set.
explanation.walkthrough: Star looks like a celebrity; it is the printed symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An asterisk is the small star-shaped typographical mark, and its name comes from the Greek for little star.

clue.text: Art exhibit popular with everybody, maybe Paddington bears?

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: to bear something is to carry it, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: Paddington is a London railway station; maybe marks it as an example
all means everybody

explanation.surface: A gallery piece featuring Paddington Bear is a hit with the public.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington evokes the marmalade-loving bear, but here it is the London terminus, and bears is the verb, to carry.
explanation.definitionFit: An installation is a large artwork built in a gallery space, so it is a type of art exhibit.

clue.text: Harry, fellow Charles admits to?

parts.note: he stands for a man or fellow

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: CR, Carolus Rex, is the royal cipher of King Charles
taken as written

explanation.surface: King Charles is asked whether he will confess to his son Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry looks like the prince alongside Charles; it is the verb, to badger.
explanation.definitionFit: To hector someone is to bully or badger them, which is what to harry means.

clue.text: Very slow climbing lower down from peak

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece placed down from another is written below it

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill or peak, as on Dartmoor

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means going upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to dip something is to lower it

explanation.surface: A sluggish climber makes slow progress going up and then coming down from the summit.
explanation.definitionFit: Torpid describes someone sluggish and inactive, as if half asleep, so moving very slowly.

clue.text: Since feeding insatiable hunger, ready to swim the Channel?

indicators.note: food goes into a mouth, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: greed is an insatiable appetite
as means since, as in as it was raining

explanation.surface: A cross-Channel swimmer eats voraciously before the attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-distance swimmers coat their bodies in grease against the cold, so a greased swimmer is prepared to set off.

clue.text: Wrong answer, with Epsom initially entered for 'horse-racing town'

indicators.note: something entered goes into a place, so this letter is put inside another word

parts.note: a sin is a wrong

indicators.note: initially points at the first letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the first letter of Epsom
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A wrong answer is given when a quiz asks which town is famous for horse racing, and someone says Epsom.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom is the English racecourse town home of the Derby, which tempts as an answer; the town wanted is Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: Siena in Tuscany stages the Palio, a famous bareback horse race around its main square twice a year.

clue.text: Half in boozer breaking taboo of some magnitude

indicators.note: breaking into something splits it open, so one piece is set inside the other

parts.note: a no-no is something forbidden, a taboo

indicators.note: half means only one of two equal parts is kept and the other discarded

parts.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub or a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: Someone half-drunk in a pub breaks an important social rule.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the back half of boozer is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-zero quantity has some size, however small, so it is of some magnitude rather than none.

clue.text: Interference from snoop gathering a bit of intelligence

indicators.note: to gather something is to take it in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: to nose about is to snoop

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a single letter of it, here its opening one

parts.note: the first letter of intelligence

explanation.surface: A spy gathers some intelligence through a bugged line full of interference.
explanation.definitionFit: Noise is unwanted signal in a radio or electronic channel, which engineers call interference.

clue.text: Greens convert Pip to cycling

parts.note: to turn someone is to convert them to another side

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so the first letter of these words moves round to the end

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An environmentalist urges someone named Pip to take up the bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: Greens look like environmental campaigners; they are leafy vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Turnip tops are the leafy upper parts of turnips, eaten as a green vegetable.

clue.text: I don't believe that story about scrapping borders!

indicators.note: about here signals that the letters are turned round, read back to front
scrapping the borders of a word removes its first and last letters

parts.note: the inner letters of story are taken

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at a tale about removing national frontiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrapping borders' strips STORY to TOR, and 'about' turns that round. The def is the exclamation of disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: Rot! is a dismissive British exclamation meaning nonsense, said of something you don't believe.

clue.text: Quickly heart someone's Instagram post

parts.note: tapping the heart on Instagram registers a like
a shot is a photograph, the kind of thing posted on Instagram

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to tap the heart on a friend's photo straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: Heart looks like a noun; it is the verb, to tap the heart icon.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a shot is an idiom meaning immediately and eagerly, as fast as a bullet.

clue.text: Run through green light then stop sign

parts.note: a green light means go
red is the signal to stop

explanation.surface: A driver goes through a junction on green and then halts at red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run through' sounds like running a red light; it means pierced, as by a bull's horns.
explanation.definitionFit: Gored means pierced by a horn or tusk, which is to be run through as by a sword.
